def: A small raised skin lesion filled with pus. Seen in acne, folliculitis and pustular psoriasis.
Located beneath the epidermis, at the dermoepidermal junction. Subepidermal blisters occur in bullous pemphigoid, in contrast to intraepidermal blisters in pemphigus.
Skin changes from chronic ultraviolet exposure, including wrinkles, leathery texture and pigment change, from damage to dermal collagen and elastin.
Describes a device, usually a coronary stent, coated with a drug that is slowly released to prevent restenosis.
Relating to the stapes, the smallest middle ear bone, or its muscle and artery.
A progestin released by the subdermal contraceptive implant (Nexplanon), which suppresses ovulation for up to three years.
A recombinant GM-CSF used to speed bone marrow recovery of white blood cells after chemotherapy or transplant.
Describes blood products from which most white cells have been filtered, lowering febrile reactions, HLA alloimmunization and CMV transmission.
Having three phalanges, as in a thumb with an extra bone. Associated with Diamond-Blackfan anemia and Holt-Oram syndrome.
People who metabolize drugs such as isoniazid, hydralazine and procainamide by N-acetyltransferase. Slow acetylators have higher toxicity risk, including drug-induced lupus.
Sloshing sound heard over the abdomen on shaking the patient, indicating fluid and air in a dilated stomach as in gastric outlet obstruction.
An irreversible proteasome inhibitor used to treat relapsed multiple myeloma.
Variables related to both an exposure and an outcome that can create a false association between them.
Painful redness, swelling and peeling of the palms and soles caused by chemotherapy such as capecitabine and fluorouracil.
Attachment of polyethylene glycol to a drug to extend its half-life, reduce clearance and lower immunogenicity.
Shrinking or return of an organ or structure to a smaller state, such as uterus after delivery or thymus with age.
Forearm muscle that pronates the forearm, innervated by the median nerve. Median nerve can be compressed between its two heads.
A long-acting monoclonal antibody against respiratory syncytial virus F protein, given to infants for RSV prevention.
Forearm muscle that supinates the forearm, innervated by the deep branch of the radial nerve, which may be compressed in radial tunnel syndrome.
Located between bones, such as the interosseous membrane of the forearm or interosseous muscles of the hand.
Thenar muscle that moves the thumb across the palm to meet the fingers, innervated by the median nerve.
A branch of L1 that supplies sensation over the suprapubic region and motor to lower abdominal wall muscles. May be injured in surgery near the groin.
Patient lying on the back with hips and knees flexed and legs supported, used for pelvic and perineal procedures and childbirth.
A thigh muscle that adducts and flexes the hip, innervated by the femoral nerve and sometimes the obturator nerve.
Normal volume of body fluid, in contrast to hypovolemia or hypervolemia.
Drugs such as probenecid that raise urinary uric acid excretion by blocking its renal reabsorption, used for gout.
Inflammation of the rib cartilages where they attach to the sternum, causing chest wall pain that is reproduced by palpation.
A CAR-T cell therapy targeting CD19, used for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Can cause cytokine release syndrome.
A monoclonal antibody against interleukin-1 beta, used for periodic fever syndromes and Still disease.
Rise in jugular venous pressure on pressing over the liver, indicating right heart failure.
Flattened membranous sacs of the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.
Around a heart valve. Perivalvular abscess is a complication of endocarditis causing conduction block.
A drug such as norepinephrine or vasopressin that constricts blood vessels to raise blood pressure in shock.
Involving the nose, sinuses and brain, as in mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis.
A dormant, highly resistant structure made by Bacillus and Clostridium species, which survives heat, drying and disinfectants.
Bacteria with shape between cocci and rods, such as Haemophilus, Brucella and Acinetobacter.
Excessive water intake with low solute intake, as in beer drinkers, causing hyponatremia.
Inanimate objects, such as towels or doorknobs, that can carry infectious agents between people.
Cell surface molecules that help a main receptor bind a ligand. CD4 and CD8 are T cell coreceptors; CCR5 and CXCR4 are HIV coreceptors.
Within the epidermis, such as the blisters of pemphigus vulgaris.
Within a joint, such as intraarticular injection of steroids.
Dark, dry scabs of dead tissue, seen in anthrax, rickettsial infections and severe burns.
A heat-stable toxin from Bacillus cereus that causes rapid-onset vomiting after eating reheated rice.
Breakdown of a polymer into its subunits, such as microtubules disassembling into tubulin.
Relating to purpura, purple skin discoloration from bleeding that does not blanch.
Restoration of function when two different mutants combine and each supplies what the other lacks, as in viral coinfection.
Rejoining of cut DNA strands, performed by topoisomerase after relieving supercoiling.
An oral drug for leishmaniasis and some free-living amebic infections.
The nonflagellated intracellular form of Leishmania or Trypanosoma cruzi inside host cells.
Describes antimalarial drugs such as chloroquine and mefloquine built on a quinoline ring.
Reinfection of the host by its own parasite without leaving the body, as in Strongyloides.
Small hooks on the scolex of tapeworms such as Taenia solium that anchor to the intestinal wall.
Severe constipation with inability to pass stool or gas, suggesting bowel obstruction.
An x-ray study of the esophagus after barium swallow.
Describes a hernia or bowel segment whose blood supply is cut off, risking gangrene.
Describes a structure that is closed or absent, as in esophageal or biliary atresia.
From a genetically different individual of the same species, as in bone marrow donated by another person.
Having detectable specific antibodies in the blood, indicating exposure or infection.
The virus family containing rubella virus.
The virus genus containing rubella virus, a togavirus-like RNA virus.
Describing an RNA genome with both positive and negative sense regions, as in arenaviruses.
